title: Chapter 160 – The First Wake
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Bell]

Bell boils the water herself.

There is a hearth in the Annex, the small cold stove in the corner that smells faintly of apples, and Nurse has lit it for the first time in more years than she will say. Bell kneels in front of it with a copper pot in her hands and watches the surface shiver, and tells herself that she is not afraid. She has delivered nine hundred infants. She has set bones in the dark and sewn up men who were already half dead. She is thirty-seven years old and has never in her life been afraid of a pot of water.

She is afraid of the pot of water.

"It will not boil faster for watching," says Nurse, from the third bed.

"I know."

"Then sit back. You are in the light."

Bell sits back on her heels. She looks down the half circle of beds, at the seven small sleeping shapes in their pale blankets, at the brass labels glinting in the lamplight, at the one empty cot at the end with its sheet turned down. The youngest is nearest the stove. Ao. A round face, a tuft of black hair, a stuffed rabbit crammed under his chin so hard that its ears stick up. She has counted his breaths every two hours for two days and knows them now as she knows her own pulse: eleven to the minute, shallow, with a catch at the top.

Three years old. For six hundred years, three years old.

"Was he a happy child?" she asks.

Nurse takes a long moment to answer. "He laughed at the lamp," she says. "The first night. When Operator Five carried him in. He saw the lamp and he laughed, and Operator Five said, There. There. He is not afraid. And I think that was the last time anyone was sure of it."

Bell nods slowly. She turns back to the pot.

The water begins to boil.

* * *

The second bed belongs to Tao, and Bell has been dreading it.

She goes to him before anything else, with the reed and the little flask of ginseng broth, and she sits on the stool beside the pillow and tips his head back with two fingers. He is five. His face is a fine small oval with a sharp chin, and the wooden top that lies by his hand has a groove worn into it by some other small hand, long ago. His lips are cracked. She wets them with a cloth first, then threads the reed past his teeth and lets the broth run down, a drop at a time, and watches his throat to see if it moves.

It does. Barely.

"Come on," she murmurs. "Come on, little spinner. One more."

His throat moves again.

She sits there for a time, with the flask warm in her palm, and counts. His breath is shallower than Ao's. His fingers are as cold as river stones. She does not like to do arithmetic about a child, but it comes anyway, unbidden, the way it always does: four days, perhaps five. If the wake of the first goes badly, perhaps fewer.

Yue has come to sit on the other side of the cot. She does not write anything. She only takes the cold little hand between her own and chafes it slowly, and breathes on the fingers, and Bell watches the tenderness in that quiet, hard-faced girl and feels her own eyes sting.

"We'll get to you," Bell says to the sleeping child. "I promise. We will get to you."

Tao does not answer. But the top beside his hand rolls a fraction, as though a draft has touched it, and settles.

* * *

She finds Jian sitting on the bridge of the stair, with his back to the wall, eating nothing.

He has the bowl in his lap and the spoon in his hand and his eyes on the middle distance, and he does not see her until she is standing over him. Then he starts, a little, and sets the spoon down. "Bell."

"Eat."

"I am eating."

"You are holding a spoon." She sits beside him, since the stairs are narrow and she is tired. For a moment neither of them speaks. Below, in the throat of the stair, the cold white mist rolls slowly past. "I have a question."

"Ask it."

"Are you afraid?"

He considers it. The answer, when it comes, is not what she expects. "Yes," he says. "Of course I am afraid. Why do you ask?"

"Because I am." She folds her hands. "I have delivered nine hundred children, Jian. I have never once been frightened at a birth. I know what to do, I know the signs, I know when to call for hot water and when to call for a priest. Tomorrow I will stand in that room and watch a child who has not drawn a breath in six hundred years draw one, and I do not know any of the signs. I do not know what to do with my hands."

"You will know."

"How can you say that?"

"Because you are Bell." He turns his head. "You have never once not known. It is the thing I have counted on, every day, since I was a boy."

She looks at him. His face is thin and deeply lined, the face of a man much older than the one she has known. She reaches out, without quite deciding to, and straightens the collar of his gown.

"You are a fool," she says.

"I know."

"Eat your broth."

He eats his broth.

* * *

They have decided to do it in the Annex, and not on the bridge.

It was Nurse who proposed it, and Ethan who agreed. The wake itself does not need Mei's presence in the shaft; it needs only her signature, which she has given, and the power of her pattern, which flows down the conduit to the beds without her lifting a finger. What it needs in the room is the Operator key, the old man with the panels in his eyes, lying on the eighth cot with his hand in the hand of the youngest child.

Bell stands at the foot of that cot and looks at what she has to work with.

Lin Jian is lying on his back with a folded cloak under his head. His face is the color of tallow. His eyes are closed, and the lids are brown and thin as paper. A thread of dark pulses in the hollow of his throat, a pulse she does not like. In his left hand, loose on the blanket, is a stuffed rabbit's paw, because Ao's hand cannot reach across the gap between the cots and Nurse has laid the rabbit between them like a bridge.

"You do not have to do this lying down," she says.

"Nurse says the key must be at rest."

"Nurse says many things." But she tucks the blanket round his feet, all the same. "How do you feel?"

"Like a very old man about to meet his brother."

"That is not an answer."

"It is the only honest one." The corner of his mouth lifts. "I am afraid, Bell. Not of dying. I am afraid he will wake and not want me."

She finds she cannot say anything to that. She puts her hand on his forehead, once, as she did when he was ill in the valley, as she has done to every patient she ever loved, and then she steps back.

"Ready," she says, to the room.

* * *

She walks the row once more before the lamps are lit, because she cannot help it.

Zhen Li, eleven, with the little brass lamp tucked into the crook of his elbow. Hai Ren, fourteen, whose long hands lie open on the blanket as though he had set something down in his sleep. The sword boy, Duan Ke, sixteen, whose label is chipped at the corner, and whose right hand is curled around nothing in particular, loosely, the way a swordsman's hand rests when he is dreaming of a hilt. The scholar, Cheng Hui, nineteen, with a red silk marker trailing out of a book of poems and the faint ink-stain of a habit on his middle finger.

She lays her palm on each of their foreheads in turn. They are cool, and smooth, and entirely untroubled. They breathe as children breathe in the first hour of sleep.

Mo Yan is last. A thin, solemn girl of eight, with a sheet of charcoal paper under her pillow. Bell lifts the corner, not meaning to pry, and finds seven small figures drawn there beneath a tree, in a firm child's hand. Six of them hold hands. The seventh, at the end, stands a little apart, with a gap left in the line beside her, as if for someone to come and fill it.

She puts the paper back very carefully.

* * *

Nurse comes to find her while she is washing her hands.

There is a basin by the wall, a plain white thing, and Bell is scrubbing her palms with a rag soaked in vinegar and bitter-root, as she always does before a delivery. She has been at it a long time. Her knuckles are red. Nurse waits until she looks up, and then holds out a folded square of cloth.

"I made this for the first one," she says. "A long time ago. I wanted to have it ready."

It is a tiny gown, no longer than Bell's forearm, in soft undyed cotton, with a drawstring at the neck and a row of small stitched ducks along the hem. The thread has yellowed. It smells of lavender.

"How long ago?"

"I started it the week he went to sleep." Nurse's round face is calm. "I finished it in the second year. I have taken it out, once a decade, and pressed it, and put it back. I told myself that it was only housekeeping."

Bell takes the gown in both hands. It weighs almost nothing.

"You were certain he would wake," she says.

"No." Nurse smiles faintly. "I was certain I would be ready if he did. They are different, you will find. It is the second that lets a person live."

Bell looks at the little ducks. She thinks of the seven small beds, of the lamps kept burning for six centuries, of a woman with a mending needle who never once allowed herself to be told it was pointless.

"Thank you," she says. She does not trust her voice for anything else.

"Put it on him when he has eaten," says Nurse, and goes to light the lamps.

* * *

It begins with a sound.

At first Bell thinks it is her own blood in her ears. A low hum, below hearing, that settles into the bones of her feet and climbs. The lamps along the curved wall dim, one after another, and then flare, brighter than before, a clean pale gold that makes every shadow in the Annex jump. The beds begin to glow. Not all of them. Only the first, the smallest, under the child with the rabbit, where a ring of fine light runs along the rail and begins to turn.

Stand back from the rail, Ethan Cole's voice says, from the grille in the wall. It is steadier than she has heard it. This will take about a quarter of an hour. Nobody should touch him unless I say.

"And if something goes wrong?"

I will say. A pause. I am sorry, Bell. I have no better answer.

She stands back.

Yue is beside her, now. The girl has come in silently and taken the place at her elbow, and her fingers are knotted in the front of her smock. She cannot hear the hum, but she can feel it; Bell sees the way she presses one palm flat to the wall, and her mouth parts a little, as though the vibration is a language she has almost learned.

On the eighth cot, Lin Jian has gone completely still.

On the first, the ring of light turns faster.

* * *

A quarter of an hour is a very long time.

Bell measures it in breaths. At the fifth minute, the light on the rail goes from gold to white. At the seventh, a thin high note rises under the hum, and Nurse's hand drops to the little bell at her belt, and Bell hears her whisper something like a prayer. At the tenth minute the stuffed rabbit's ears twitch, and for one dreadful second she thinks it has come alive. It has not. The child's hand beneath it has moved.

"Nurse."

"I see."

The small fingers curl. They close around the rabbit's paw, and the paw, which is also in Jian's hand, tightens, and for a moment the old man and the sleeping child are holding the same toy.

The glow shivers.

And from the grille, in a voice Bell has not heard before, a small clear girl's voice says, quite calmly, Papa, it's starting to hurt.

Ethan makes a sound like a cry. Mei—

It's all right. It's not too much. It's like a tooth.

Bell's whole body clenches. She wants to stop it. She wants to cross the floor in four strides and pull the old man's hand away from the child's, and she knows she cannot. The wake is a held thread; if she cuts it, she does not know what falls.

Twelve percent, says Ethan, tight and low. She's at twelve. Fourteen. Please, please, Mei, tell me if it's too much—

It's okay, Papa. I can do the rest.

* * *

Bell has watched people die. It is the oldest of her skills and the one she likes least. She has learned its signs: the sharpening of the nose, the dulling of the eye, the blue that creeps under the nails. She knows what the end of a life looks like.

She has never seen the opposite.

The first thing she sees is color. A faint rose creeping into the cheek of a child who has been gray as ash for two days. Then the breath: a long, slow, wet sigh, and then another, deeper, and then a sudden ragged gasp, like a swimmer coming up out of deep water. The small chest heaves. The mouth opens. The eyelids flutter, and flutter, and tremble open on two dark, wet, bewildered eyes.

Ao looks at the ceiling.

For a long moment he does not move. His gaze goes up and up, tracing the curve of the dome, the high window with no view, the lamps that have all gone to a soft gold. His lip trembles. His fingers tighten on the rabbit, and he makes a tiny sound in his throat, a lost small sound, the sound of a child who has woken in a strange room and cannot find his mother.

Bell does not think. She is across the floor before she knows she has moved, and on her knees beside the cot, and her hands are out in front of her, palms up, open, empty, the way she has learned to hold them for children who are afraid.

"Hello," she says. "Hello, little one. It's all right. I'm Bell."

The dark eyes find her face.

"I'm a healer," she says, and her voice is not steady, and she lets it be unsteady. "I'm going to sit right here. You don't have to say anything. You can look at me as long as you want."

Ao looks at her. He looks for a long time.

Then, with the grave dignity of a child of three, he says, in a cracked little voice that has not been used in six hundred years: "Where's Papa?"

* * *

Bell cannot answer. She only holds out her hand.

The child takes it.

His fingers are warm. That is what she will remember afterward, and what she will remember when she is as old as the man on the next cot: that the hand she is holding is warm, and small, and strong, and that it is gripping hers as hard as it can.

"He's here," says a voice from the wall. "Ao. I'm here."

The little head turns. The dark eyes go to the grille.

"Papa?"

"Yes. Yes, sweetheart. I'm here. I'm just—" The voice breaks. Bell can hear him trying to hold it level and failing. "I'm just a little way off. I'll come as soon as I can. Do you see the lady? Her name is Bell. She is a friend."

Ao considers Bell with great seriousness.

"Is she a nurse?"

"Almost."

"I have a nurse," says Ao. He looks over her shoulder, past the stove, to where the small round woman in the apron stands with both hands pressed to her mouth. His face transforms. It is not a smile. It is something larger. It is the face of a child who has found the one fixed point in an unfamiliar world.

"Nurse," he says.

Nurse makes a sound that Bell will never forget. She crosses the floor with her skirts clutched in both fists, and kneels, and gathers the child into her arms with the rabbit between them, and her whole body shakes.

"I mended him," she is saying, over and over. "Eleven times. I mended him."

* * *

When the weeping has eased, Nurse brings the broth.

It is only rice water at first, thin and warm in a white cup, and she feeds it to the child on the tip of a small wooden spoon. Ao takes it gravely. He watches the spoon, not the cup, and each time it comes toward him he opens his mouth just a little wider than necessary, a trick Bell has seen in many small children and never understood. He swallows. He frowns at the taste.

"Is it nasty?" Bell asks.

"It's wet," says Ao, with feeling.

She laughs. It surprises her, a bright astonished crack of sound in the quiet room, and Nurse laughs, too, through her tears. Ao looks from one to the other and gives a solemn little nod, as though a point has been conceded.

"Where is my top?" he asks.

"That's Tao's, sweetheart. Yours is the rabbit."

"I know." He holds it up and inspects the stitching, the faded patch of felt on one ear, the place where the thread has been renewed with a slightly different color. "He's been mended."

"Yes."

"Lots of times."

"Eleven."

He thinks about this. Then, to Bell's surprise, he lifts the rabbit to Nurse's cheek and presses it there for a moment, the way a child gives a kiss.

"Thank you," he says.

Nurse closes her eyes.

From the grille in the wall, very quietly, Ethan Cole says, Twenty-two.

Bell looks up. "Twenty-two what?"

Percent. What it cost her. I wanted you to know, now that it is done. She is awake. She is asking whether the little one liked the rabbit. A pause, and a sound that may be laughter, may be something else. I told her he did. She says she is glad. She says she is a little dimmer, and not to worry.

Bell does not answer. She cannot. She looks at the small boy in Nurse's arms, solemn and pink-cheeked and alive, and thinks of the girl in the well, and finds that there is no sum in the world that comes out even.

* * *

Yue catches her sleeve at the door.

The girl has her slate, and she has been waiting, Bell thinks, a long time. She writes quickly, in the poor light, and holds it up.

Is he going to be all right? The old man?

"He is exhausted," Bell says. She keeps her voice level, and speaks to the girl's face, and lets her read the words. "He has spent himself for forty days, and the wake took more than he had to give. I will not lie to you. He is not well."

Yue's jaw tightens. She wipes the slate with her wrist.

How long?

"I do not know." That is true, and she says it plainly. "If he rests, and eats, and does not walk another step, perhaps a year. Perhaps more. If he goes on as he has been, I could not say. Not many months."

The girl does not weep. She stands very straight, staring at the chalk on her palm, and Bell sees the thing that moves in her face, something old and hard that is learning to bear weight.

He won't rest, Yue writes at last. Not with two more beds.

"No."

Then we have to make sure there are no more beds that need him.

"Yue—"

Teach me how to do what you do. Her eyes lift, fierce and clear. The reed. The broth. How to count a pulse. If I can sit with Tao, you can sit with him.

Bell looks at the girl for a very long moment. Then she puts her arm round the thin shoulders and says, "Come. I will show you."

* * *

Lin Jian has not stirred.

Bell notices it late, and it is a sickness in her. She turns from the little bed and the weeping woman, and crosses to the eighth cot, and puts two fingers to the old man's throat.

The pulse is there. Faint. Uneven. Like a bird against a window.

"Jian." She touches his cheek. "Jian. Wake up."

The lids tremble. His mouth moves. She bends close, and he says, in a voice like a dry leaf, "Is he...?"

"Awake. He's asking for his nurse. You did it."

A breath that might be a laugh. "Good."

"You are an idiot," she says, fiercely, and wipes her eyes with the back of her wrist. "You are the worst patient I have ever had, and you did it, you stubborn old man. Now lie still while I look at you."

His eyes open. They are clear, with a faint blue light moving behind them. He looks past her to the first bed. Ao is sitting up in Nurse's arms, studying the room with the cautious gravity of the very young, and as Jian watches, the boy turns his head and looks straight at him.

The old man smiles.

Ao does not smile back. He is looking, Bell realizes, not at the face, but at something just past it. He is looking at the faint blue light.

"You have the blue," says Ao.

Nobody breathes.

"I'm sorry?" Bell says. "The what?"

"The blue." Ao's small face has changed. The bewilderment has gone out of it, all at once, and in its place is something fixed and watchful and far too old. "He has the blue in his eyes. Number Eight."

"Ao—" Nurse says, very low.

"Hello, Eight." The childish voice is the same. The tilt of the head is the same. But the words come slow and clear and level, like a thing being read from a page. "Operator One. Awake. Acknowledging."

Jian has gone rigid on the cot.

"Priority message," says the child. "Stored in the First Wake, to be delivered upon the Eighth's arrival. Do you hear me, Eight?"

"I hear you," says Jian, hoarsely.

"The Wall is not enough." The dark eyes are unblinking. "The beasts are already on the Seam. They have smelled the Hall. They are coming up from below, and there are more of them than the Wall can hold, and I am sorry, Brother, but you have perhaps sixty days."

Behind Bell, in the wall, the voice of Ethan Cole whispers, very softly: Oh, no. Oh, my boy. I forgot I wrote that.

And in the Annex, the lamps flicker, once, and every one of them goes dim.
